title: The Table Set Before Opponents
english: To be more watery.
The part of the humanization overflows.
When someone 'beholds his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (John 1:14), the wine overflows.
Therefore, he prepared this table not near the one being called, nor far from him, but before him and in front of those distressing him.
The apostle, turning this enigma to something clearer, writes: 'For a large and effective door has been opened to me, and many are standing against me' (1 Cor 16:9).
When someone has a word and a door of a word strong and effective, he has many standing against him.
And the devil himself stands against, wishing to prevent the benefit from the effectiveness of the word, as do sophist men and other evil men.
Not so much, indeed, do they stand against, as having once attacked the one working well.
'In front of those distressing me' he prepared the table.

He once said concerning that saying about the infant Jesus: 'For before knowing how to call father or mother, he will receive power over Damascus and the curs of Samaria in the presence of the king of the Assyrians' (Isa 7:6).
It was not a great thing if the curs took things while the king of kings was absent, but in front of him, while he was present, they snatched what he had under himself.
Or did he not plunder the magi in front of the king of the Assyrians?
For they were in the act of practicing magic.
They did not come to the child having previously repented, but while the demons were still active.

Such a thing, indeed, has been seen ecclesiastically, that those, having done their usual things in calling demons, not sparing them, recognized that the magic was dissolved from the child signified by the appeared star.
Having come, therefore, to me, such a thing, these distressing ones were present, and in their very faces the things of the blessing happened.
The 'in front of' can also be thus: they were present in opposition of will, wishing to prevent what is for them, or wishing to harm him. 'I anointed my head with oil' (Ps 23:5).
You showed me Christ; according to what is signified it is said:
'Touch not my anointed ones' (Ps 104:15).
And this holy one was one of the anointed, of those anointed 'with oil of gladness beyond his fellows' (Ps 44:8)—of Christ.
The man himself was anointed beyond his fellows, beyond the other anointed ones, concerning whom it has been said:
'You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones' (Hab 3:13).
'You anointed' then 'my head with oil' (Ps 22:5).
In many places the head signifies the mind;
as when it is said:
'The wise man's eyes are in his head' (Eccl 2:14).
Indeed, common usage also says that the more foolish have no brain, have no head.
The ruler of a system is called the head of the system.
Since then the mind also rules and leads our whole composition, it is called head.
And many scriptures teach this, which we have often mentioned.
He did not say simply 'was anointed,' but 'with oil';
for there is also worthless oil, concerning which the holy one prays, saying:
'let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head' (Ps 140:5).
'And your cup intoxicating, as excellent' (Ps 22:5).
Since not everyone can drink the whole mixing-bowl which wisdom mixed (Prov 9:2), he distributes to each a cup, which receiving, he can be gladdened.
Some copies have:
'and my cup';
which you have given me.
However, it is said either way.
'Intoxicating,' then, is 'as excellent'.
It brings the drinker excellent intoxication—sober intoxication.
And 'intoxicating' is instead of 'gladdening'.
We often call the wine-bibber drunk.
And even the mere touching and tasting is called intoxication.
And they etymologize intoxication thus:
in ancient times there was no abundance of wine, when immediately the fruit of the vine was found making wine, and in feasts and public festivals they drank after sacrificing.
They did not drink at another time.
And for this reason it is called intoxication.
And intoxication often signifies merely touching:
'they shall be intoxicated from the fatness of your house' (Ps 35:9), instead of 'they are gladdened';
for intoxication is spoken of differently, with reproach:
